title: A Tel1-Rad9 axis links DNA double-strand break end-tethering to repair pathway choice.

verified.what_i_actually_checked: Downloaded and parsed the full open-access text (Europe PMC XML, 182 KB) and read the data availability statement, the whole Materials and Methods, and every mention of a supplementary item. Ran the project's paper_context tool: it found no accessions in the text other than three Protein Data Bank entries reused from other papers (6S8F, 6JXA, 6JXC), no GEO/SRA/BioProject/BioSample links, and no Zenodo or Dryad record for the DOI. Two attempts at the Europe PMC supplementary-file endpoint both timed out at 135 s, so the supplement itself could not be opened.
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: The contents of the supplement are known only from the article text: Supplementary Figures S1-S11 and four tables (S1 yeast strain genotypes, S2 primers for gene disruption and tagging, S3 oligonucleotides for quantitative PCR, S4 a narrative summary of the main phenotypes of the strains). No machine-readable measurement table is described anywhere.

a1_downloadable.note: Data availability says only 'available in the article and in its online supplementary material' - no repository, no accession. The supplement is presumably free to download from the publisher, so no login or application is needed, but I could not retrieve it (Europe PMC supplementary endpoint timed out twice at 135 s), so this passes unverified.

a2_label_is_a_column.note: FAILS. There is no data table at all, so no prediction target column. Every quantity in the paper (percent of cells with tethered DNA break ends, fold enrichment of Tel1 at the break by chromatin immunoprecipitation, percent single-strand-annealing versus crossover repair products, resection efficiency from gel densitometry) exists only as bars and blots inside figure images. A label would have to be built by digitising figures or re-running the yeast experiments.

a3_inputs_present.note: No feature table either. The only machine-readable inputs would be the Tel1 protein sequence and three public Protein Data Bank structures; the experimental 'inputs' are yeast strain genotypes written as free text in Supplementary Table S1.

a4_units_stated.note: Units are stated clearly in the methods (percentages, fold enrichment, hours after break induction, micromolar drug concentrations) - but they describe figure panels, not columns in a file.

a5_enough_rows.note: FAILS. The unit of measurement is a yeast strain x genotoxin x timepoint combination; the paper reports on the order of a few dozen strains with three biological replicates each. That is two to three orders of magnitude below the ~1,500 labelled rows the checklist requires. Exact count not verifiable because Supplementary Table S1 could not be opened.

a6_fits_laptop.note: Everything in the paper, including the supplement, is far under a gigabyte; size was never the problem here.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: Cannot be assessed: there are no counts to compare because there is no deposited file. Recorded as a fail only in the sense of being unverifiable, not as a discrepancy.

a8_label_provenance.note: The measurements that do exist are genuine wet-lab readouts (fluorescence microscopy of tagged break ends, chromatin immunoprecipitation with quantitative PCR, Southern blots), not another model's output. The molecular-dynamics and AlphaFold 3 structural models are predictions, but they are used as illustrations, not as labels.

existing_models.name: inDelphi, FORECasT and Lindel (machine-learning predictors of CRISPR/Cas9 repair outcomes)
existing_models.score_and_split: Reported correlations between predicted and observed repair-outcome distributions of roughly r = 0.56-0.85 depending on cell line, from a comparison found in search results; splits were held-out target sites, not held-out labs.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Not read - only search-result summaries were retrieved, so I am not quoting a discussion section.

existing_models.name: Boolean network model of double-strand break repair pathway choice (Journal of Theoretical Biology)
existing_models.score_and_split: A rule-based dynamic simulation of homologous recombination, classical end joining, single-strand annealing and microhomology-mediated end joining; not a fitted statistical model, so no held-out score.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Not read beyond the search-result summary.

backbone.name: ESM-2 (a protein language model) would be the natural fit for Tel1 variant effects
backbone.hardware: CPU is enough, but there is nothing to fit a head on - the paper supplies one mutant allele, not a mutational scan.

integration.partner_dataset: None usable. UniProt (Tel1/ATM entries) and AlphaFold DB could be joined on a UniProt accession, but with roughly one variant of interest there is nothing to join.
integration.join_key: UniProt accession (P38110, yeast Tel1) - the paper never lists it in a column.
integration.bigger_question_one_sentence: Cannot be written: a join between one hand-made yeast allele and a large protein resource adds no new question.

controls.positive_control: Not applicable - no model was scored.

honest_claim_h3: No honest machine-learning claim is possible from this paper: it reports a mechanism (a Tel1 FAT-domain variant that boosts Rad9 phosphorylation and oligomerisation, keeping broken DNA ends together and shifting repair from single-strand annealing toward strand-invasion recombination) using a few dozen yeast strains, with every number living inside a figure.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use yeast mutant genotype and protein-variant sequence to predict which DNA-break repair route the cell takes.
plain_idea.train_on: What I considered: one row per yeast strain (its mutated genes, plus the Tel1 protein sequence with its substitutions) crossed with the time after a DNA break was induced. The paper supports roughly a few dozen such strains; I could not verify the exact number because the strain table would not download.
plain_idea.predict: The share of DNA breaks repaired by single-strand annealing versus strand-invasion recombination, and how close the two broken ends stay to each other. Both come from wet-lab readouts: Southern blots of repair products and fluorescence microscopy of two fluorescently tagged spots flanking the break.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: If it worked, DNA-repair labs could rank candidate mutants before building strains. But at this scale a table of the measurements would already answer the question, so a model adds nothing.

more_or_better_data.why: The paper contributes a few dozen strains measured in one lab; the CRISPR repair-outcome models were trained on tens of thousands of sequenced target sites. There is no dimension on which this is bigger or better.

confidence_score.why: Three biological replicates per strain do give a noise estimate, but with only a few dozen groups there is no way to fit, let alone calibrate, per-prediction uncertainty.

models_beatable.why: The adjacent models (inDelphi, FORECasT, Lindel) solve a different task - predicting insertion/deletion patterns at CRISPR cut sites in human and mouse cells - and nothing in this yeast paper could be fed to them or compared against them.

guaranteed_improvement.why: Fails on every condition: no baseline can be run on this data, our model would not see what theirs sees, the assays measure different quantities in different organisms, and no shared split exists.

ml_idea: No viable machine-learning project. The underlying biology (what decides whether a cell repairs a DNA double-strand break by annealing or by strand invasion) is genuinely interesting and under-modelled, but this paper supplies a mechanism and a handful of strains, not a dataset. A real project on this question would need a published genome-wide screen or a deep mutational scan of Tel1/ATM, not this article.

effort.compute_note: No compute estimate is meaningful because no feature/label table can be built; the only numbers would come from digitising figure panels by hand.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: Read the data availability statement and count the deposited files - it took five minutes and killed the project: 'available in the article and in its online supplementary material', with the supplement being eleven figures and four strain/primer tables.

verdict_reason: A classical small-scale yeast genetics paper with no deposited dataset. It fails checklist item A2 (the thing to predict is not a column anywhere - every measurement is a bar or a blot inside a figure), A3 (no feature table) and A5 (a few dozen strains, far under the ~1,500-row floor). Nothing about the files contradicts the paper; there simply are no data files.
